SUMMARY 
This report recommends that City Council state its intention to designate the property at 
70 Gerrard Street East under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its 
cultural heritage value according to the Statement of Significance which includes a 
description of heritage attributes found in Attachment 1. 
The subject property at 70 Gerrard Street East is located on the north side of Gerrard 
Street East, at the northeast corner of Church Street, within the Downtown Yonge East 
neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. 
A location map and current photograph of the heritage property are included in 
Attachment 2. 
Constructed c. 1845 and substantially altered in 1886 according to plans by Langley & 
Burke, the property historically known as the Dr. James Elliot Graham House contains a 
remodelled Queen Anne Revival style, two-and-a-half-storey detached house-form 
building, which was originally designed in the Georgian style. Following its long tenure 
as a private residence, the subject property has since the 1970s been home to a series 
of commercial and institutional establishments and organizations, including Egerton's 
Restaurant, The Edge music venue, and Under 21/Covenant House. The property 
forms part of a group of surviving mid- to late-19-century house-form buildings around 
the intersection of Church Street and Gerrard Street East, in the east section of 
downtown Toronto. 
The subject property at 70 Gerrard Street East was listed on the City of Toronto's 
Heritage Register on March 15, 1974. 
This property is one of eighteen pre-1870 listed properties citywide which have been 
identified as candidates for designation through the City's implementation of Bill 23 
amendments to the Ontario Heritage Act and its ongoing prioritization strategy for listed

evaluation of design/physical value, historical and associative value and contextual 
value.  A property may be designated under Section 29 of the Act if it meets two or 
more of the provincial criteria for determining whether it is of cultural heritage value or 
interest.

STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE 
(REASONS FOR DESIGNATION) 
The property at 70 Gerrard Street East is worthy of designation under Part IV, Section 
29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural heritage value and meets Ontario 
Regulation 9/06, the provincial criteria prescribed for municipal designation. 
Description 
The subject property at 70 Gerrard Street East is located at the northeast corner of 
Gerrard Street East and Church Street, within the Downtown Yonge East 
neighbourhood of downtown Toronto. Constructed circa 1845 and substantially altered 
in 1886, the property contains a two-and-a-half-storey detached house-form building, 
originally built in the Georgian style and remodelled in the Queen Anne Revival style. 
The property forms part of a group of surviving mid- to late-nineteenth-century house-
form buildings around the intersection of Church and Gerrard Streets, in the east 
section of downtown Toronto. 
Statement of Cultural Heritage Value 
Design and Physical Value 
The property at 70 Gerrard Street East has design and physical value as a 
representative example of a mid-19th-century detached house-form building designed in 
the Georgian style and remodelled in the Queen Anne Revival style. Popular in Ontario 
in the closing decades of the 19th century, the Queen Anne Revival style was 
classically rooted but more ornamental and freer in its use of decoration than the 
Georgian and later Edwardian styles, and is characterized by picturesque, irregular 
massing, varied rooflines, projecting bays and dormers, and the use of varied materials 
and ornament. The style lent itself readily to the updating of earlier, plainer houses, 
allowing a restrained Georgian dwelling to be given a fashionable and richly modelled 
appearance. At 70 Gerrard Street East, the 1886 remodelling of the earlier circa 1845 
Georgian house retained the underlying two-and-a-half-storey form while overlaying it 
with a more varied roofline and massing, projecting bay windows, dormer windows, 
bargeboard, and brackets. 
The property also has design and physical value for the high degree of craftsmanship 
and artistic merit displayed in its exterior detailing. The projecting bay windows, 
pedimented and gabled dormers, ornamental bargeboard, dentillated cornice, 
decorative brick spandrel panels, and the turned and bracketed woodwork of the 
entrance demonstrate the skilled brickwork and carpentry associated with fine domestic 
architecture of the period, and the skillful application of ornamentation by the 
architectural practice of Langley & Burke.

Historical and Associative Value 
The property at 70 Gerrard Street East has historical and associative value through its 
long association with Dr. James Elliot Graham (1847–1899), a prominent Canadian 
physician, researcher, and teacher of the late 19th century, who owned and lived at the 
property from 1875 until its sale in 1890, after which he continued to reside at and 
conduct the bulk of his medical practice from the house until 1895. Graham made 
significant contributions to clinical research and medical pedagogy in Canada while 
residing at 70 Gerrard Street East, was elected president of the American 
Dermatological Association in 1888, served as Professor of clinical medicine at the 
University of Toronto, and held the presidencies of the Toronto Medical Society, the 
Toronto Pathological Society, the Ontario Medical Association, and the Canadian 
Medical Association. 
The property also has associative value through its later use, from 1978 to 1981, as The 
Edge, an influential live-music venue in the development of Toronto’s underground punk 
and new-wave scene. Programmed by Gary Topp and Gary Cormier, the venue hosted 
a wide range of international and local performers and formed part of the emergence of 
Toronto’s late-20th-century live-music culture. 
The property has further associative value through its role, from the early 1980s, as the 
first Toronto Under 21 Centre of Covenant House and, subsequently, as Mary’s Home 
operated by the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul. Covenant House was established in 
New York City in 1972 to serve the city’s homeless youth and arrived in Toronto in 1982 
with 70 Gerrard Street East serving as the organization’s intake centre and medical 
facility before moving nearby to 20 Gerrard Street East. Afterwards, the building was 
used for similar purposes as Mary’s Home and continues to provide services to 
vulnerable members of the community. These uses reflect the long-standing character 
of the downtown east section of Toronto as a centre for religious and secular institutions 
serving vulnerable and lower-income members of the community. 
Finally, the property has associative value as a work of the Toronto architectural firm of 
Langley & Burke, one of the leading architectural practices in the city in the late 19th 
century, which designed the 1886 remodelling of the house into its present Queen Anne 
Revival form. Langley & Burke operated from 1883 to 1892, producing numerous 
ecclesiastical and residential commissions. Their expertise and proclivity with the 
Queen Anne Revival style, as seen at 70 Gerrard Street East, is reflected in the 
commissions they executed in and around Jarvis Street and the Annex in the late 19th 
century, one example being the J.H. McKinnon House (1888) at 506 Jarvis Street. 
Contextual Value 
The property at 70 Gerrard Street East has contextual value as it is important in 
defining, maintaining, and supporting the historic character of the Church and Gerrard 
Streets area. The subject property forms part of a collection of mid- to late-19th-century 
house-form buildings around the intersection of Church and Gerrard Streets that 
together maintain a fine-grained, pedestrian-scaled, streetscape characteristic of the 
19th-century neighbourhood. Anchoring the northeast corner of Church and Gerrard, 
the property supports this historic character amid the taller, later development that has 
replaced much of the surrounding fabric.

3. RESEARCH 
This section of the report describes the history, architecture and context of the property. 
Visual resources related to the research are located in Section 4. Archival and 
contemporary sources for the research are found in Section 5 (List of Sources). 
Indigenous Communities 
For time immemorial, Toronto has been home to Indigenous peoples. Ojibway oral 
histories speak of Ice People, who lived at a time when ice covered the land.1 Following 
the retreat of glaciers approximately 13,000 years ago, small groups of Indigenous 
peoples moved from place to place, hunting and gathering the food they needed 
according to the seasons. Over millennia, they adapted to dramatically changing 
environmental conditions, developing and acquiring new technologies as they did 
so. Waterways and the lake were vital sources of fresh water and nourishment, and 
shorelines and nearby areas were important sites for gathering, trading, hunting, fishing, 
and ceremonies. Long-distance trade moved valuable resources across the land. 
After maize and squash were introduced to Southern Ontario, by approximately 500 CE, 
horticulture began to supplement food sources. By 1300 CE, villages focused on 
growing food became year-round settlements surrounded by crops. These villages were 
home to ancestors of the Huron-Wendat Nation, who would continue to occupy 
increasingly larger villages in the Toronto area and beyond. These villages were 
connected to well-established travel routes which were part of local and long-distance 
trail networks, including the Carrying Place trails on the Don, Rouge and Humber rivers 
that connected Lake Ontario to Georgian Bay. Beads made from seashells from the 
eastern seaboard were found at the Alexandra site in North York, which was a 
community of 800-1000 people in approximately 1350. 
By 1600, the Wendat had formed a confederation of individual nations, and had 
concentrated most of their villages away from Lake Ontario, in the Georgian Bay area. 
Following contact with French explorers and missionaries in Southern Ontario in the 
early 1600s, European diseases decimated First Nations. Competition for furs to trade 
with Europeans and the desire to replenish numbers through absorption of captives, 
among other factors2, contributed to the Beaver Wars, which after 1640, saw the 
Haudenosaunee Confederacy expand into Southern Ontario, dispersing the Wendat. 
Within the boundaries of today's Toronto, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy then 
occupied villages on the Carrying Place trails on the Humber and Rouge Rivers from 
approximately the 1660s to the 1680s. 
In the late 1680s, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy chose to leave their village in the 
Toronto area and returned to their homelands in upstate New York. As evidenced by the 
1701 Great Peace of Montreal, the 1701 Nanfan Treaty, and the Dish with One Spoon 
Treaty, the Haudenosaunee continued to have an interest in the resources of the area.

Anishinaabe people from the Lake Superior region then moved into the Toronto area. 
While the Wendat and Haudenosaunee people lived in year-round villages surrounded 
by crops, the Anishinaabe people continued to live primarily by seasonally moving 
across the land to hunt, fish and gather resources that were available at a specific time, 
including migrating birds and maple syrup. To the west of Toronto, the Anishinaabe 
people became known as the Mississaugas of the Credit. To the east, they became 
known as the Chippewas of Beausoleil, Georgina Island and Rama and the 
Mississaugas of Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha, Scugog Island.3 
In 1787, as the British began to prepare for an influx of colonists into the area following 
the American Revolution, the British Crown negotiated the Toronto Purchase with the 
Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation to obtain title to the land. The flawed and poorly 
documented agreement was invalidated, and Treaty 13 was negotiated in 1805 for 
lands now including much of the City of Toronto. In 1923, the Governments of Ontario 
and Canada signed the Williams Treaties for over 20,000 km2, including portions of 
eastern Toronto, with seven First Nations of the Chippewa of Lake Simcoe (Beausoleil, 
Georgina Island and Rama) and the Mississauga of the north shore of Lake Ontario 
(Alderville, Curve Lake, Hiawatha and Scugog Island). 
The Mississaugas, Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee, or the Wendat did not traditionally 
regard land as a commodity to be sold. Following the Toronto Purchase, the British 
government quickly set out to survey the land into lots which were either sold or granted 
into private ownership of settlers. In 2010, the Government of Canada settled the 
Toronto Purchase Claim with the Mississaugas of the Credit after agreeing that the 
Mississaugas were originally unfairly compensated. In 2018, the Williams Treaties First 
Nations settled litigation about land surrenders and harvesting rights with the 
Governments of Canada and Ontario. 
The City of Toronto remains the traditional territory of many nations including the 
Mississaugas of the Credit, the Anishnabeg, the Chippewa, the Haudenosaunee and 
the Wendat peoples and is now home to many diverse First Nations, Inuit and Métis 
peoples. Toronto is also covered by Treaty 13 signed with the Mississaugas of the 
Credit, and the Williams Treaties signed with seven Mississaugas and Chippewa First 
Nations. 
i. HISTORICAL INFORMATION 
The following section outlines the history and facts related to the properties which are 
the basis for determining historical or associative value of Criteria 4, 5 or 6 according to 
O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
Park Lot 7 
In 1793, Park Lot 7 was granted to the British military officer Captain John McGill (1752-
1834). McGill had previously served under John Graves Simcoe in the American 
Revolutionary War, after which he settled in Upper Canada before arriving in York 
(Toronto) where he was appointed to the Legislative Council in 1797 and as Lieutenant

of the County of York in 1805.4 In 1803, McGill constructed a house on Park Lot 7 
looking south to Queen Street East, south of present-day Shuter Street. 
McGill died in 1834, and, owing to his lack of a direct heir, his estate was inherited by 
his nephew, Peter McCutcheon, on the condition that he would assume the surname 
McGill. McCutcheon was at that time a merchant newly appointed to the position of 
President of the Bank of Montreal; it was from his seat in Montreal that he proceeded to 
sell-off the lands still held within Park Lot 7. In 1836, a Plan of Subdivision was filed 
encompassing land from Lot Street (Queen Street East) to Gerrard Street East and from 
Yonge to Jarvis Street, maintaining McGill Cottage and Garden on the land occupied 
today by Metropolitan United Church, and establishing the contemporary street pattern. 
70 Gerrard Street East 
In 1845, Peter McGill sold Lot 18 within Plan 22A comprising the northeast corner of 
Church Street and Gerrard Street East to John Attlay Smith.5 In 1846, John Attlay Smith 
is listed in the city directory as a dry goods merchant residing at the northeast corner of 
Church and Gerrard. Smith’s store is listed at 81 King Street East, which formed the 
western edge of Victoria Row designed by the architect John Howard and built in 1843. 
In 1849, McGill sold Lot 19 immediately to the east to Mr. Smith as well. 
By 1861, John Smith appears to have ceased running a dry goods store and is shown in 
the census as a gentleman, 68 years old, residing in a two-and-a-half-storey brick 
house with his wife Eliza Dignan, two school-aged sons (F.D. and Edwin A.) and three 
servants. The Smith family continued to reside at 70 Gerrard Street East until 1871, 
when John passed away. Eliza sold lots 18 and 19 in 1875 to Dr. James Elliot Graham. 
Dr. James Elliot Graham (1847-1899) 
Dr. James Elliot Graham was a Canadian physician, researcher, and teacher who made 
significant advancements in the field of clinical research, medical pedagogy, and the 
professionalization of private research and consulting within his field. Graham was born 
in Richview, Ontario and educated at Upper Canada College and the Toronto School of 
Medicine before receiving an MB and MD from the University of Toronto. He pursued 
his interest in the field of medicine internationally, with time spent in Brooklyn, New York 
followed by Germany, Vienna, and London, where he became a licentiate of the Royal 
College of Physicians, before returning to Toronto in 1872. His classmate at the Toronto 
School of Medicine, Sir William Osler, remained a close friend for the next thirty years.6 
Upon return, Dr. Graham first appears in the city directories at 336 Yonge Street, south 
of Elm Street.7 In 1873, he married Mary Jane Aikins, daughter of the politician James 
Cox Aikins who sat in cabinet for Sir John A. Macdonald following Confederation and 
was serving as Secretary of State for Macdonald at the time of their wedding.8 In 1875,

at the Toronto General Hospital (then located at Gerrard Street East and Sackville 
Street) and assumed a teaching position at the Toronto School of Medicine. 
Graham transitioned from private practice to consultancy around 1880, pursuing a 
range of interests in service of Toronto's and North America’s growing medical fields. 
Graham served important positions with the Toronto Medical Society, the Toronto 
Pathological Society, the Ontario Medical Association, and the Canadian Medical 
Association, as well as serving two terms on the senate of the University of Toronto. In 
1888, he was elected president of the American Dermatological Association, and from 
1887, was Professor of clinical medicine at the university. 
In 1885, Dr. Graham commissioned the architectural practice of Langley & Burke to 
design alterations and an addition to 70 Gerrard Street East. He had in the late 1870s 
sold off portions of Lot 19, and had the same firm design a townhouse at 74 Gerrard 
Street East, which he leased to doctors. The 1886 alterations (Figures 6 & 7) converted 
the Georgian house into a more fashionable Queen Anne Revival home; the primary 
(south) façade was improved with three large bay windows on the second floor, a 
revised roof profile with dormer windows and a pedimented gable, and a more ornate 
primary entrance. On the west façade and rear they added a gabled bay and addition, 
permitting additional living space and private quarters. The redesign provided for a 
drawing room, waiting room, and surgery on the first floor, alongside a formal dining 
room, with three bedrooms and a nursery on the second, and a basement kitchen. 
Dr. Graham’s health began to deteriorate in the early 1880s due to diabetes, which he 
managed while maintaining a successful consulting medical practice; in 1887, he 
established the Ontario Medical Library Association, which merged with the Toronto 
Academy of Medicine in 1907. In 1890, Graham sold 70 and 74 Gerrard Street East to 
William Proudfoot Caven, however continued to reside at 70 Gerrard Street East until at 
least 1895.9 In 1899, Graham contracted pneumonia, exacerbating his pre-existing 
diabetes, and subsequently died while in Muskoka in July of that year. City directories 
show that Dr. Graham was residing at 134 Bloor Street East at the time of his death. 
Ownership of 70 Gerrard Street East remained with William P. Caven until 1922, before 
being sold to Albert S. Rogers. By 1970, city directories indicate that the property had 
been subdivided into three apartments, and by 1974 was converted into a restaurant 
and bar. 
Langley & Burke, Architects 
Henry Langley (1836-1907) was one of Toronto's most prolific and successful 
architects. In addition to his architectural output, Langley was committed to advancing 
the cause of the architectural profession as he participated in the founding of the 
Canadian Institute of Architects in 1876, the establishment of the Architectural Guild of 
Toronto in 1887, and the formation of the Ontario Association of Architects in 1889.

Henry Langley was a partner in three significant practices: Langley & Langley; Langley, 
Langley & Burke; and Langley & Burke, whose collective works spread across Ontario. 
The firm of Langley, Langley & Burke was one of the most highly regarded and 
influential architectural partnerships of High Victorian Toronto. They were well-known for 
their ecclesiastical work as well as several important public commissions. The firm was 
composed of Henry Langley (1836-1907), his brother, Edward Langley, a builder, and 
their nephew Edmund Burke (1850-1919). Edmund Burke was born in Toronto and 
apprenticed with Gundry and Langley in the late-1860s and formed partnerships with his 
uncles Henry and Edward Langley in the 1870s and 80s. The firm of Langley, Langley & 
Burke lasted from 1873 to 1883 when Edward moved to California and afterward 
continued as the firm of Langley & Burke. 
Burke and Langley together were prolific in designing dozens of important ecclesiastical 
works in Ontario during their 1873-1892 practice. Their work included landmark Toronto 
churches such as the Jarvis Street Baptist Church (1874-75), Sherbourne Street 
Methodist Church (1886-87), and Trinity Methodist Church (1887-89) as well as a broad 
array of significant residential, commercial, and institutional buildings. 
Burke was known for his versatility and application of new building technologies, 
particularly his precedential use of shingled cladding that later became widely used in 
several suburban districts, like the Annex. In several of their commissions, Langley & 
Burke were heavily influenced by British architect Richard Norman Shaw, who 
popularized the Queen Anne Revival style. This style was reflected in other homes that 
arose in the vicinity of Jarvis Street, establishing their approach to prominent residential 
commissions in the late 19th century. 
Burke left the firm Langley & Burke in 1892 to take over the practice of William George 
Storm after his death. A short time later in 1894, he partnered with Horwood to form the 
firm of Burke and Horwood. An architect whose hundreds of commissions extended 
across Canada, Burke was the subject of a monograph in 1995, Redefining Canadian 
Architecture: Toronto Architect Edmund Burke, by Angela Carr. Burke is remembered 
for the instrumental role he played in founding regulatory organizations in Canada, 
which led to legal recognition of professional status for Canada's architects by codifying 
standards of practice and education. 
Egerton’s Restaurant and The Edge 
In 1974, the subject property opened as Egerton’s Restaurant, a popular student 
restaurant and coffee shop named for Egerton Ryerson, who at the time was purported 
to have lived at 70 Gerrard Street East, however no primary sources support such a 
claim. Egerton’s was on the periphery of Yorkville’s folk music scene, lacking the size 
and concentration of similar nearby venues to become a fixture on the scene, but 
through proximity to Ryerson University (now TMU) became a popular student hangout. 
As the coffee house culture diminished, Egerton’s owners, including manager Ron 
Chapman, saw an opportunity to re-orient the venue with a focus on underground music 
and tapped Gary Topp and Gary Cormier, known as The Garys, to book musical acts. 
The Garys were well-known in the Toronto music scene, having launched the New 
Yorker Theatre on Yonge Street (now the CAA Theatre), and booked shows at the 
70 Gerrard Street East - Notice of Intention to Designate Page 18 of 29

Horseshoe Tavern.10 In 1978, they were invited to revitalize Egerton’s, relaunching the 
venue, which they playfully renamed as The Edge, on December 31st, 1978, with a 
show by Martha and the Muffins. 
From 1978 until its closure in 1981, The Edge was a fixture of Toronto’s burgeoning 
underground music scene. The venue was “…an exploding black box inside a colonial 
historic building. Sometimes the vibe was chilled by free jazz, folk legends, or blues 
artists, but the dominant sound was a mix of crunch post-punk and British new wave.”11 
The venue was known for booking both international and local acts, hosting Nico, Joan 
Jett, Simple Minds, Sun Ra, The B-52s, XTC, Rough Trade, and The Police in an 
intimate 200-person capacity venue (Figure 11). 
By 1981, The Edge was running into financial challenges, unable to balance the wear 
and tear of a live music venue at night with an operating restaurant during the day and 
hosted its final show in June 1981. 
Although short-lived, The Edge fits within a trajectory of live music venues in Toronto as 
underground punk, rock, and new wave acts moved from small restaurants and clubs to 
larger venues, including The Diamond Club (1984); Lee’s Palace (1985); and Massey 
Hall. The Edge was a reflection of Toronto’s growing diversity and increasing 
prominence in the international music scene, attracting an audience that was “…a mix 
of in-the-know Queen Street types, queer art-school kids, and people who came from all 
over Southern Ontario to see bands that often played nowhere else in the region.”12 
Under 21/Covenant House 
In the early 1980s, 70 Gerrard Street East was sold to the Roman Catholic Church to 
serve as the first Toronto Under 21 Centre, an initiative of Covenant House. Under 21 
was founded by Father Bruce Ritter, a New York City Franciscan friar who established a 
ministry in the city's Lower East Side in 1968 to serve the city’s homeless youth and 
teens. Branded as Covenant House in 1972, the ministry provided group homes and 
counselling aimed at getting youth off the streets and out of the drug and sex trade.13 
Covenant House and the Under 21 Centres that it ran steadily grew in popularity with 
the charismatic Father Ritter at the helm, expanding in New York City, other states, 
Central America, and Canada. 
Gerald Emmett Cardinal Carter, Archbishop of Toronto from 1978 to 1990, saw a need 
in Toronto to provide refuge for the city’s homeless youth and petitioned for funds from 
the church and community to bring Covenant House to Toronto. The funds raised were 
used to purchase and extensively renovate the subject property at 70 Gerrard Street 
East as an intake centre and medical facility, with a 30-bed residence at 179 Gerrard

In December 1989, Father Ritter was accused of sexual impropriety and resigned under

were laid; however, an independent investigation commissioned by the Covenant

70 Gerrard Street East continued to operate as Covenant House until the mid-1990s; in 
1994, the charity purchased the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union and Willard Hall 
at 20 Gerrard Street East to expand their intake, residential, and educational programs. 
70 Gerrard Street East was transferred to the Society of St Vincent de Paul, a Roman 
Catholic charitable organization founded in 1833 with roots in Toronto dating to 1850. 
The Society reorganized 70 Gerrard Street East as Mary’s Home, opening in 1996 as a 
women’s shelter providing long-term housing, an emergency dorm, and Out of the Cold 
programming. Mary’s Home has since transitioned solely into an emergency shelter and 
continues to provide critical services to vulnerable women in the community.17 
ii.  ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
The following section provides an architectural description and analysis related to the 
property which will establish the basis for determining design or physical value of 
Criteria 1, 2 or 3 according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The subject property at 70 Gerrard Street East contains a two-and-a-half-storey 
detached house form building constructed circa 1845 with significant alterations and 
additions in 1886 lending it its present-day appearance (Figure 14). The primary (south) 
façade fronting on Gerrard Street East is organized into three bays and clad in red brick 
with buff brick pilasters. The central bay contains the primary raised entrance, with brick 
stairs leading to a rectangular opening with inset wood door frame containing a double 
entrance door bound by narrow sidelights. The entrance is protected by a wooden 
awning with shed-style roof clad in asphalt shingles, painted wooden railings and 
banisters, and turned columns featuring wooden brackets supporting the awning. A 
decorative wooden balconet protrudes from the awning and supports the second-floor 
bay window above. Rectangular window openings with splayed stone lintels bound the 
primary entrance in either bay on the first floor. The second storey features protruding 
bay windows with decorative panels dating to the 1886 Langley & Burke alterations. 
The hipped roof features a pedimented cross-gable dormer in the central bay, with 
pedimented gabled dormer windows on either side. A dentillated cornice wraps the 
roofline, with bargeboard trim ornamenting the cross-gable dormer and shading an 
arched window opening.

iii. CONTEXT 
The following section provides contextual information and analysis related to the 
property which is the basis for determining contextual value of Criteria 7, 8 or 9 
according to O. Reg. 9/06 Criteria. 
The City of Toronto Property Data Map attached (Attachment 2) shows the site of the 
property at 70 Gerrard Street East. 
The subject property is located on the north side of Gerrard Street East at the northeast 
corner of Church Street, within the Downtown Yonge East neighbourhood. The land 
was subdivided from Park Lot 7 – the former estate of Captain John McGill – under the 
1836 Plan of Subdivision and formed part of a residential district laid out in the mid-19th 
century and built up through the second half of the century with a mix of row, semi-
detached, and detached houses, together with churches, schools, and other institutions. 
The detached house-form structure located at 70 Gerrard Street East forms part of a 
collection of mid- to late- 19th century house-form buildings around the intersection of 
Church and Gerrard, including 66 Gerrard Street East (1855, listed); 74 Gerrard Street 
East (1885, Part IV designated); 76 & 78 Gerrard Street East (1858, Part IV 
designated); 322 Church Street (1847, Part IV designated); and 418 Church Street 
(1891, Part IV designated). Collectively, these properties maintain a fine-grained, 
pedestrian-scaled streetscape that characterized the 19-century neighbourhood, with 70 
Gerrard Street East anchoring the northeast corner of Church and Gerrard amid the 
taller, later development that replaced much of the surrounding historic fabric (Figure 
15). 
Since the mid-20th century, Toronto's downtown east end has been home to vulnerable 
and lower-income communities, along with associated social services including 
Covenant House. The long-term presence and operation of secular and religious social 
service organizations, many of which reside within repurposed historic buildings 
including 20 and 70 Gerrard Street East, has been an important neighbourhood staple, 
reflecting the present-day diversity and fabric of the broader community.
